I don't think you understand what I mean by "hidden variables". A hidden variable is like a dice roll, or drawing a card from a deck, or RNG in a videogame. It's a value that is difficult or impossible to predict with accuracy and isn't known until it is revealed. Any time you have a hidden variable, luck/randomness is involved because the game state is perpetually incomplete causing you to have to guess.

A game of chess or go has no hidden variables because the entire state of the game can be seen by all players at any given point in time.

The term you're looking for is incomplete information games. And you're wrong. Incomplete information simply requires different strategies for optimal play. You're not guessing but you begin to play a strategy that requires a consideration of nondeterministic forks - eg A can lead to B, C, or D instead of A always leading to B. There are optimal strategies in these situations and there are unoptimal strategies. The thing that gets you from the from the latter to the former is skill. In many ways games with randomness result in an even wider range of skill levels than complete information games since humans pretty much suck at intuitively understanding randomness - we always see patterns, even when none exist.

I think this isn't so much a question of minimizing luck rather as not limiting skill. Games with optimal strategies that are relatively trivial to approach tend to end up being pure luck since everybody approaches near optimal play easily at which point luck is the sole differentiator. High skill ceilings on the other hand mean skill ends up being the primary differentiator. Another issue is sample size. So for instance poker in the longrun is close to 100% skill. Poker in the short run is almost exclusively luck.

There are games without randomness or hidden information and without skill either, games with both and games with one or the other. The notion of skill is human-defined, randomness and hidden information isn't, they aren't comparable.
